## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.92820.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.92820.3.sa3)

Summary:

In the manuscript titled "Hemispheric Divergence of Interoceptive Processing Across Psychiatric Disorders", the authors analyzed a subset of data collected for a larger project investigating interoception in anorexia nervosa and generalized anxiety disorder (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02615119). This study utilized fMRI and various analyses with a special focus on the insula and its connectivity to map the neural commonalities and differences in both top-down and bottom-up interoceptive processing.

The primary aim was to compare whether these neural activations were quantitatively and qualitatively different in a sample of healthy controls (HC) versus patients diagnosed with anxiety, depression, and/or eating disorders (ADE).

The study initially recruited 70 patients with primary diagnoses of ADE and 57 HC. After applying exclusion criteria, the final sample consisted of 46 ADE patients and 46 matched HC. Participants underwent task-related and resting-state fMRI scan sessions.

Specifically, participants performed 2 tasks in fMRI: (i) a bottom-up interoceptive (ISO) task involving intravenous infusions of isoproterenol (a peripherally-acting beta-adrenergic receptor agonist) administered in a double-blind, placebo-controlled fashion to alter cardiovascular activity where participants were asked about their visceral awareness; and (ii) a top-down interoceptive attention (VIA) task where participants were asked to focus on their visceral sensations triggered by words indicating specific body parts (e.g., STOMACH, HEART, LUNGS) or to pay attention to color changes of the word TARGET during an exteroceptive control task.

Main results show overlapping patterns of neural activation within the dysgranular mid-insula during top-down and bottom-up interoceptive processing with hemispheric differences. The patterns of dysgranular activation distinguished individuals with ADE compared to HC. Also differences in the activation of the anterior agranular insula during periods of interoceptive uncertainty differentiate ADE patients from HC.

Strengths:

- This is a very nice study that aligns with modern Clinical Neuroscience approaches, as recommended by NIH policy (i.e. RDoC initiative), which puts emphasis describing clinical conditions via transdiagnostic dimensions measured on psychological processes, behaviors, and neural processes rather than merely identifying a series of symptoms.

I appreciated very much the different analyses that authors performed to characterize differences at the qualitative and quantitative regarding the insular activity and its connectivity during bottom-up and top-down interoceptive processes.

These findings may open avenues for new studies that will explain the mechanisms underlying these phenomena and provide useful insights for developing novel interventions.

Weaknesses:

Weakness/Requests of additional clarifications

(1) The sample

(1.1) The authors describe the patient's group as having a primary diagnosis of anxiety, depression, and/or eating disorders. However, Table 1 shows that the majority had Anxiety disorders, some Major Depression (it is not clear which are the percentages of patients that at the time of the study had a concurred problem of major depression, please clarify), and very few had a diagnosis of Anorexia Nervosa. The leftward activation asymmetry and distinct activation patterns in the left dysgranular mid-insula across both the ISO and VIA tasks found on ADE did not correlate with symptoms measured by the SCOFF questionnaire, but correlated with anxiety and depressive symptoms. It would be nice if the authors can comment on these results in relation to eating disorders.

(1.2) Furthermore, the sample consisted of 5 males and 41 females in the HC group and 1 male and 45 females in the ADE group. In order to generalize these findings, the authors should acknowledge this gender imbalance and discuss whether they expect similar results in a predominantly male sample.

(2) The procedure

While the fixed order of tasks reflects the primary emphasis on acquiring data from the infusion (ISO) task, this could introduce confounding order effects. The authors should acknowledge this as a limitation of this study.

(3) The rationale behind the study

- The authors recognized that there was a broader aim behind this data collection. It would be important to clarify a little bit more how the differences in insular areas mapping both (or specifically) bottom-up and top-down interoceptive processes and insular connectivity, recorded in ADE patients compared to healthy controls (HC), contribute to psychiatric diagnoses (hypothesis 3).

For example, they should explain the psychopathological dimensions common to the three patient groups. Are disturbances in bottom-up and top-down interoceptive processing common traits in these patients, reflected in the asymmetric interhemispheric dysgranular mid-insular activation? The link between these disturbances and anatomical evidence of convergence/divergence of top-down vs. bottom-up interoceptive processes should be clearly stated.

(4) Operationalization of Convergence / Divergence maps underlying top-down and bottom-up interoceptive processes in HC vs ADE patients

It is not clear to me the concept of Convergence / Divergence maps underlying top-down and bottom-up interoceptive processes. The authors want to compare, in HCs and ADE patients, the neural structures that are co-activated (convergence maps) vs those that are uniquely involved (divergence maps) in top-down and bottom-up interoceptive processes in the two groups. Thus, I would expect that these two different analyses would have been performed on similar portions of data, instead different moments of the tasks (=different bottom-up / top-down interoceptive processes) have been analyzed.

Specifically, the convergence maps have been identified by comparing active voxels recorded when participants were focusing on the heart and the lungs (compared to when they were focused on the exteroceptive features of the target) in the VIA task, and during infusions (Peak period) of 2mcg isoproterenol (compared to baseline) in the ISO task. The divergence maps have been identified by comparing voxels uniquely active during the anticipatory phases of both isoproterenol and saline infusions (compared to baseline) and during the peak period of saline dose of the ISO task with respect to when participants focused their attention on the heart and the lungs (compared to when they were focuses on the exteroceptive features) in the VIA task.

I understand the idea of mapping interoceptive uncertainty, however I think that these two analyses do not show commonalities and differences in the neural structures involved in bottom up vs top down processes (in ADE vs HC), but also neural correlates underlying different types of interoceptive processes involving or nor top-down expectations.

According to the authors, which is the most important neural marker that differentiates the ADE group: the difference in hemispheric activations within the left and right dysgranular insula or the less granular anterior insular activation during periods of interoceptive uncertainty? Also, do they reflect different transdiagnostic dimensions?

(5) Collected physiological measures

The authors speak about cardiorespiratory interoceptive processes, but they only included cardiac measures. Including respiratory changes could provide a more comprehensive comparison between bottom-up signals and top-down attentional processes. Also, I guess that the "STOMACH" trials of the VIA task were not analyzed in this study since those are used in the bigger study and since no gastric measures were collected? Please clarify this point.

(6) ISO task instructions

To better understand the task and participants' expectations, could the authors clarify the instructions given to participants regarding the isoproterenol and saline infusions. Did the participants have two types of expectations?

(7) Title of the study

I understand that the term "divergence" in the title refers to the different hemispheric activations characterizing ADE patients compared to HC. However, it also suggests an analysis based on convergence/divergence maps, which might be ambiguous. Could the authors make some small modifications to the title to make it clearer?

(8) Caption of Figure 7

The caption of Fig.7 notes that no difference in HR was found during the Saline infusion between the HC and ADE groups. However, it would be fair to mention the significant difference in dial ratings observed during the Saline infusion. How do the authors explain this difference?

Typos

Figure 3 In Figure 3, "Hemispheric divergence", I think, should be corrected to "Hemispheric convergence."

I believe that by addressing these points, the manuscript will provide a clearer and more comprehensive understanding of the rationale, methods, and findings underlying this study.

results.result: The study addresses a gap in the literature by investigating the neural interface between top-down attention and bottom-up visceral inputs in interoceptive processing. While each process has been independently associated with psychiatric symptomatology, the neural substrates of their interaction were previously unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C59 establish the theoretical background and identify a clear gap in knowledge that the study addresses. These are well-supported by citations to prior work and accurately characterize the state of the field.

results.result: The study employed a preregistered design with 46 ADE and 46 propensity-matched HC participants, using two neuroimaging tasks to manipulate top-down attention (VIA task) and bottom-up interoceptive signals (ISO task with isoproterenol infusions). Three primary hypotheses were tested regarding dysgranular mid-insula co-activation, agranular anterior insula selectivity to uncertainty, and lateralized differences in the ADE group.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C8 and C60-C63 describe the study design, which is clearly documented with appropriate methodological detail. The preregistration and propensity matching strengthen the rigor of the approach. The experimental manipulations are well-justified.

results.result: After quality control, 46 participants per group were propensity-matched on age, sex, and BMI. Groups did not differ on these variables but showed expected differences in clinical measures (anxiety, depression, eating disorder symptoms). The ADE group exhibited high comorbidity (67% GAD, 72% depression, 35% anorexia nervosa) and most were taking psychiatric medications.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C73 describe the sample characteristics with appropriate statistical documentation. The propensity matching successfully balanced demographic variables while preserving clinical differences. However, the high medication use and comorbidity in the ADE group could be confounds that are not fully addressed.

results.result: Neural activation converged upon the dysgranular mid-insula bilaterally across both the ISO and VIA tasks, confirming the dysgranular mid-insula as a key interface between top-down attention and bottom-up interoceptive processing. This finding corroborates previous independent studies of each task.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C74-C75, and C125-C127 describe the primary convergence finding with supporting neuroimaging data (Figure 2, Table 2). The anatomical localization using cytoarchitectonic atlases strengthens the specificity of the finding. This directly addresses the study's main hypothesis.

results.result: The ADE group exhibited hemispheric asymmetry in dysgranular insula activation patterns, with increased left and decreased right dysgranular co-activation compared to HC. Spatial similarity between groups was lower in the left (Dice=0.58) than right (Dice=0.78) hemisphere. This supports the left dysgranular mid-insula as a 'locus of disruption' in psychiatric disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13, C76, C79-C80, and C128-C129 describe group differences with quantitative metrics (chi-square tests, Dice coefficients). The hemispheric asymmetry is well-documented and connects to prior meta-analytic findings (Nord et al., 2021). However, the mechanistic interpretation remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Despite spatial differences, activation magnitude in convergent dysgranular regions did not differ between groups. However, right hemisphere activation was greater than left during interoceptive processing in both tasks, and right dysgranular activation correlated with subjective cardiorespiratory sensations (r=0.21, p=0.046).
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 report statistical findings with appropriate tests and effect sizes. The right hemisphere dominance is specific to interoceptive conditions (C83). The correlation with subjective perception (C84) is modest but significant, though the lack of correlation with objective physiological measures raises questions about what the activation represents.

results.result: Activation in convergent dysgranular regions during perturbation was not associated with objective heart rate changes, retrospective intensity ratings, state anxiety, or trait anxiety sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C89 report null findings with appropriate statistical tests. These null results are important for interpretation but raise questions about the functional significance of the observed activation patterns. The lack of association with trait measures is particularly notable given the clinical focus.

results.result: Post-task resting state functional connectivity between right dysgranular insula and left middle frontal gyrus increased in the ADE group only. This connectivity change correlated with trait anxiety (r=0.36-0.43) and depression (r=0.38) but not with physiological or perceptual responses during the task.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C95 describe connectivity findings with appropriate corrections for multiple comparisons. However, the lack of a temporal control condition (acknowledged by authors) limits interpretation of whether changes are task-specific or reflect general time effects. The correlations with clinical measures are moderate but the directionality and mechanism remain unclear.

results.result: The agranular anterior insula was selectively activated during periods of interoceptive uncertainty (Anticipation and Saline Peak) but not during the VIA task, with activation increasing from Anticipation to Saline Peak and showing right hemisphere dominance during Saline Peak. The ADE group showed reduced spatial extent of this activation, particularly in the right hemisphere during Anticipation.
results.evaluation: Claims C14 and C96-C110, C132-C134 describe the divergence analysis with appropriate statistical documentation. The selective activation during uncertainty periods supports a prediction-generating role for the agranular insula, distinct from the dysgranular convergence. However, the lack of correlation with anxiety sensitivity (C111) is unexpected given the theoretical framework.

results.result: Agranular insula activation magnitude was not related to trait anxiety sensitivity in either epoch or hemisphere when examined transdiagnostically.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 reports a null finding with appropriate statistical tests. This is surprising given the theoretical link between uncertainty processing and anxiety, and may suggest that spatial extent rather than magnitude is the relevant metric for clinical differences.

results.result: During isoproterenol infusion, both groups showed large heart rate increases with minimal group differences (significant only at 98-99s). However, the ADE group reported significantly higher subjective cardiorespiratory sensations during the latter Peak and Recovery periods (110-142s). During saline, heart rate remained at baseline in both groups, but HC showed slightly higher dial ratings than ADE.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 describe physiological and perceptual responses with cluster-based permutation testing. The dissociation between objective (minimal group difference) and subjective (prolonged ADE elevation) responses is important and well-documented. The reversed pattern during saline (HC>ADE) is intriguing but less well-explained.

results.result: Retrospective ratings showed no group differences in cardiac or respiratory intensity for either ISO dose, but ADE reported greater anxiety following both infusions. During the VIA task, ADE reported higher cardiac intensity but lower exteroceptive intensity, with no differences in lung or stomach sensations.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C124 report behavioral findings with appropriate statistical tests. The dissociation between real-time and retrospective ratings is notable. The VIA task findings suggest modality-specific differences in interoceptive versus exteroceptive attention in the ADE group.

results.result: The findings confirm the dysgranular mid-insula as a key cortical interface where attention and prediction meet real-time bodily inputs, especially during heightened interoceptive awareness. The dysgranular mid-insula may be a 'locus of disruption' for psychiatric disorders, with hemispheric imbalance concurrent with heightened perceptual responses and altered functional connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 and C130-C131 represent interpretive conclusions that extend beyond the direct data. While the convergence finding (C16) is well-supported, the characterization as a 'locus of disruption' (C18) is more speculative and based on correlational evidence. The concurrent relationships (C130-C131) are observed but causal mechanisms remain unclear.

results.result: The study found convergent neural activation in the dysgranular mid-insula during both top-down interoceptive attention and bottom-up cardiorespiratory perturbation tasks. This convergence was localized bilaterally to the granular and ventral dysgranular subregions, supporting the dysgranular mid-insula as a key cortical interface where attention and prediction meet real-time bodily inputs.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirmed this finding. Reviewer 1 stated the work 'reveals convergent activation largely localised to the ventral dysgranular subregion,' Reviewer 2 noted 'convergent activity within the granular and dysgranular insular cortex,' and Reviewer 3 described 'overlapping patterns of neural activation within the dysgranular mid-insula.' The editor called this 'compelling evidence for dysgranular insular involvement.'

results.result: The ADE group exhibited hemispheric asymmetry in dysgranular insula activation patterns, with increased co-activation in the left dysgranular insula and decreased co-activation in the right dysgranular insula relative to healthy controls. Spatial similarity between groups was lower in the left (Dice=0.58) than right (Dice=0.78) hemisphere.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirmed this finding. Reviewer 1 noted 'convergent activation...differs in extent between patients and controls,' Reviewer 2 described 'a patient group-specific lateralisation effect,' and Reviewer 3 acknowledged 'leftward activation asymmetry and distinct activation patterns in the left dysgranular mid-insula.' The editor confirmed this 'corroborates the assumption that the mid-insula may indeed be a locus of interoceptive disruption.'

results.result: The agranular anterior insula showed selective activation during periods of interoceptive uncertainty (anticipation and saline infusion periods), with activation increasing from anticipation to saline peak. This pattern was similar between groups spatially but the ADE group showed less activation during bodily uncertainty periods.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this finding. Reviewer 1 stated the work 'reveals different extents of divergent activation in the anterior insula during anticipation of interoceptive disruption,' and Reviewer 3 noted 'differences in the activation of the anterior agranular insula during periods of interoceptive uncertainty differentiate ADE patients from HC.' The finding aligns with the pre-registered hypothesis about uncertainty processing.

results.result: Post-task resting-state functional connectivity between the right dysgranular insula and left middle frontal gyrus increased in the ADE group only, and this connectivity change was associated with trait anxiety and depression severity across the entire sample.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raised concerns about this finding, stating 'the interpretation of the resting-state isoproterenol data could potentially represent fluctuations over time rather than following interoception specifically' and recommended 'future studies should investigate test-retest reliability of this measure.' However, the reviewer noted 'this does not preclude the strong conclusions which can be drawn from the authors' task-based data.'

results.result: Activation magnitude in convergent dysgranular regions showed no group differences but demonstrated right hemisphere dominance during interoceptive processing. Right dysgranular activation during peak perturbation correlated with real-time cardiorespiratory sensations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these findings. The hemispheric dominance and correlation with subjective perception are presented as supporting evidence for the main convergence findings, and no reviewer raised concerns about these specific quantitative results.

results.result: During isoproterenol infusion, the ADE group showed heightened perceptual responses (dial ratings) during the peak and recovery periods despite minimal differences in objective heart rate changes. During saline infusion, HC showed slightly higher dial ratings than ADE despite no heart rate differences.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically requested clarification about the saline dial rating differences, asking 'How do the authors explain this difference?' This indicates the reviewer accepted the finding but sought interpretation. No reviewer challenged the validity of these behavioral results, and they are integrated into the broader interpretation of heightened interoceptive sensitivity in ADE.

results.result: Retrospective ratings showed the ADE group reported greater anxiety following both isoproterenol and saline infusions, higher cardiac intensity during heart-focused attention in the VIA task, but lower exteroceptive intensity ratings. No group differences emerged for retrospective cardiac/respiratory intensity or excitement ratings.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these behavioral findings. Reviewer 3 noted the leftward activation asymmetry 'correlated with anxiety and depressive symptoms,' implicitly accepting the symptom severity measures. These findings support the broader clinical characterization of the ADE group.

results.result: The study used a pre-registered design with 46 ADE patients and 46 propensity-matched healthy controls, employing two tasks: a voluntary interoceptive attention task (VIA) and a pharmacological perturbation task (ISO) using isoproterenol. The sample was predominantly female with high psychiatric comorbidity in the ADE group.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raised concerns about generalizability, noting 'the transdiagnostic patient sample was almost entirely female, and many were currently taking psychotropic medications; future studies should replicate these effects in unmedicated, sex-balanced samples.' Reviewer 3 requested clarification about the sample composition and asked authors to 'acknowledge this gender imbalance and discuss whether they expect similar results in a predominantly male sample.' Reviewer 3 also noted the fixed task order 'could introduce confounding order effects.'

results.result: Neural activation in convergent regions during perturbation was not associated with objective physiological arousal (heart rate changes), post-scan ratings of cardiac/respiratory intensity, state anxiety, trait anxiety sensitivity, or dial ratings. Agranular insula activation was not related to trait anxiety sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these null findings. They are presented as part of the comprehensive analysis showing that right dysgranular activation specifically correlated with real-time perception but not with other measures, supporting the specificity of the main findings.

results.result: The study addressed a gap in knowledge about the neural substrates where top-down attention and bottom-up visceral inputs interface to produce conscious interoceptive perceptions. Three pre-registered hypotheses predicted dysgranular mid-insula co-activation, agranular anterior insula selectivity for uncertainty, and lateralized differences in the ADE group.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 stated 'The work is strongly theory-driven, building on and directly testing results from influential theories and previous studies.' Reviewer 3 appreciated that the study 'aligns with modern Clinical Neuroscience approaches' and noted the pre-registered hypotheses. All reviewers acknowledged the study filled an important gap, with Reviewer 1 noting 'these functions of the insula in interoception and mental health have never been compared directly before.'

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the primary convergence finding in the dysgranular mid-insula (C9-C10, C74-C75, C125-C127). OpenEval emphasizes anatomical specificity using cytoarchitectonic atlases, while peer reviewers explicitly affirmed this as 'compelling evidence.' Peer review also includes interpretive claims C16-C17 which OpenEval addresses separately in R13.

Perfect agreement on group differences and hemispheric asymmetry (C11-C13, C76, C79-C80, C128-C129). Both evaluations support these findings with OpenEval noting the connection to prior meta-analyses while acknowledging speculative mechanistic interpretation. Peer reviewers consistently affirmed the lateralization effect and its clinical significance.

Complete agreement on divergence analysis findings (C14, C96, C100, C105-C110, C132-C134). Both support the anterior agranular insula activation during uncertainty periods. OpenEval notes the unexpected lack of correlation with anxiety sensitivity (C111), which peer reviewers did not specifically challenge.

Full agreement on hemispheric dominance and correlation findings (C81-C84). Both evaluations support these results. OpenEval raises questions about the lack of correlation with objective physiological measures, while peer reviewers accepted these findings without challenge as supporting evidence for main conclusions.

Complete agreement on behavioral findings (C118-C124). Both support the dissociation between real-time and retrospective ratings and the VIA task findings. Peer reviewers implicitly accepted these results as part of clinical characterization, while OpenEval explicitly notes the modality-specific differences.

Strong agreement on physiological and perceptual responses (C112-C117). Both support these findings. OpenEval emphasizes the dissociation between objective and subjective responses. Peer review includes C130 (interpretive claim) and notes Reviewer 3 requested clarification about saline differences, indicating acceptance with interest in interpretation.

Both evaluate connectivity findings (C90-C93) with uncertainty. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to lack of temporal control condition limiting interpretation of task-specificity. Peer Reviewer 1 similarly raised concerns about whether findings represent 'fluctuations over time rather than following interoception specifically,' recommending future test-retest reliability studies.

Both support the theoretical background and knowledge gap (C1-C3, C59). OpenEval affirms these are well-supported by citations. Peer reviewers praised the theory-driven approach, with Reviewer 1 noting the study 'directly testing results from influential theories' and fills an important gap. Peer review also includes study design claims C61-C63.

Both address sample characteristics (C64-C73) but with different emphases. OpenEval supports the statistical documentation while noting medication use and comorbidity as potential unaddressed confounds. Peer reviewers rated UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about generalizability due to predominantly female sample, medication use, and fixed task order. Peer review also includes study design claims C4-C8, C60.

Partial overlap on study design claims (C4-C8, C60). OpenEval R2 supports the methodological rigor including preregistration and propensity matching. Peer R8 rates UNCERTAIN due to concerns about sample composition (gender imbalance, medication) and fixed task order, which OpenEval addresses separately in R3 regarding sample characteristics.

Both support null findings (C85-C89) as valid results. OpenEval notes these raise questions about functional significance and the lack of trait measure associations. Peer reviewers accepted these null results without challenge, viewing them as supporting the specificity of main findings regarding right dysgranular activation.

Both support the null finding regarding anxiety sensitivity correlation (C111). OpenEval finds this surprising given theoretical links between uncertainty and anxiety. Peer reviewers accepted this as part of comprehensive analysis showing specificity of correlations with real-time perception but not other measures.

Divergent evaluations of interpretive conclusions (C16-C18, C130-C131). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting that while convergence is well-supported, characterization as 'locus of disruption' is speculative based on correlational evidence. Peer reviewers included C16-C17 in their SUPPORTED evaluation of the convergence finding, with the editor calling it 'compelling evidence' for dysgranular insular involvement.

OpenEval evaluated connectivity findings C94-C95 (correlations with clinical measures) as UNCERTAIN due to unclear directionality and mechanism. These specific claims were not separately evaluated by peer reviewers, though C94-C95 appear in peer R9's list of accepted null findings.

Minor overlap on study design claims (C61-C63). OpenEval R2 supports the preregistration and experimental manipulations as part of overall methodological rigor. Peer R10 supports the theory-driven approach and pre-registered hypotheses as filling an important gap in the field.
